report:
Based on the strongest available evidence, the answer is actually **yes**, not no — regular CT screening does reduce lung cancer mortality in heavy (ex-)smokers. This is one of the best-established findings in cancer screening research, so I want to flag that clearly before summarizing.

## Findings

Two major randomized controlled trials provide high-quality evidence:

**NLST (National Lung Screening Trial, USA):** In 53,454 current/former heavy smokers aged 55–74 (≥30 pack-years, quit ≤15 years if former smokers), annual low-dose CT screening reduced lung cancer mortality by **20%** compared with chest X-ray screening (https://www.cancer.gov/types/lung/research/nlst).

**NELSON trial (Netherlands/Belgium):** In high-risk men and women, volume CT screening reduced lung-cancer mortality by roughly **24–26%** in men over 10 years, with an even larger benefit (up to 33–41% in some analyses) in women, confirming and strengthening the NLST result (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1911793; https://pressroom.cancer.org/NELSON2020).

Subsequent meta-analyses, including pooling with the smaller UK Lung Cancer Screening (UKLS) trial, confirm a statistically significant mortality reduction from LDCT screening (https://www.iaslc.org/iaslc-news/press-release/ukls-trial-meta-analysis-confirms-low-dose-ct-screening-lung-cancer). A 2021 USPSTF-commissioned systematic review in JAMA likewise concluded that LDCT screening reduces lung cancer mortality, while also causing false positives, overdiagnosis, and incidental findings that require careful management (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2777242).

## Conclusion

The randomized-trial evidence (NLST, NELSON) consistently shows that regular low-dose CT screening **does** reduce lung cancer mortality among heavy current/former smokers, by roughly 20–25%, at the cost of manageable harms (false positives, overdiagnosis, radiation exposure). This is why USPSTF and other bodies recommend it for high-risk smokers. You may want to revisit your assumption that the answer is "no."
